LESSONS.title: Say hi with print
LESSONS.goal: Show text on the screen with print
summary: print shows what's inside the ( ) on screen
Wrap text in quotes, front and back
One print, one line, top to bottom

cards.say: Let's start our first code with a hello! print is a command that shows whatever you put inside its parentheses on the screen. Wrap text in quotes, front and back.
Use print several times and you get one line each, in the order you wrote them. Like a barista reading an order slip from the top. An empty print() prints one blank line.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Quotes only mark “the text starts here and ends here,” so they don't show on screen. Only the text inside the parentheses appears.

items.q: Fill in the blank so “Sunny today” appears on screen.
items.explain: Python treats uppercase and lowercase as different letters. It only understands print written all in lowercase.

items.q: Which code shows “Snacks” without an error?
items.explain: Text needs quotes that open and also close. Without quotes, Python goes hunting for something named Snacks and gives an error.

items.q: Put the lines in order so the steps for cooking ramyeon (Korean instant noodles) print correctly.
items.expect:
1. Boil water
2. Add noodles
3. Add soup powder
items.explain: print runs in the order you write it. The order of lines in your code is the order of lines on screen.

items.q: How many lines appear on screen when you run this code?
items.explain: An empty print() prints one blank line with nothing on it. So it's A, a blank line, then B: 3 lines.

items.task:
Let's make a bus stop sign! Use print twice to print these two lines exactly.
Next bus: No. 152
Arriving soon
hints: Count how many lines you need to print. The colon and spaces must match the example exactly, too.
print prints one line at a time, and text goes in quotes. Think back to the first card.
Write one print for the first line and one print for the second line, one under the other.

print("___")
print("___")
items.explain: Two prints printed two lines in the order you wrote them. You put the colon and spaces inside the quotes exactly, so it matches the sign.

items.q: Which statement about print is true?
options: It shows what's inside the ( ) on screen
It shows the quotes on screen too
You can write it in capitals, like Print
items.explain: print shows what's inside the parentheses, and quotes only mark where text starts and ends. The name must be all lowercase.

LESSONS.title: Working with strings
LESSONS.goal: Join strings together and repeat them
summary: Characters wrapped in quotes make a string
+ joins strings with no space between
string * number repeats it that many times
f"…{math}…" puts a result into a string

cards.say: A bunch of characters wrapped in quotes is called a string. Double quotes and single quotes both work. Just start and end with the same kind.
You can join strings with +. Multiply a string by a number with * and it repeats that many times. Doing math on words sounds a little fishy, but it's really handy.
Put an f before the quotes and you can put math inside { }. The result pops right in between the words. Forget the f and the { } shows up as plain text.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: + joins two strings exactly as they are. It doesn't add a space between them.

items.q: Fill in the blank so “Rain is coming” appears.
items.explain: If you want a space, you have to put it inside the string yourself. And quotes open and close with the same kind.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Multiplying a string by a number repeats it that many times. The copies come out stuck together, with no spaces.

items.q: Fill in the blank so “HaHaHa” appears.
items.explain: You repeat with the multiply sign *. A string and a number are different kinds of things, so + between them causes an error.

items.q: Which of these causes an error?
items.explain: If you open with a single quote, you close with a single quote. When they don't match, Python can't tell where the string ends.

items.q: Put the lines in order for a menu: title, divider, then gimbap (Korean rice rolls).
items.explain: "=" * 6 made the divider, and + joined the menu name and price. Line order is screen order.

items.q: Fill in the blank so “3 umbrellas” appears.
items.explain: The f before the quotes calculates what's inside { }. With r, the { } prints as plain text, and x is a letter Python doesn't know there, so it's a SyntaxError.

items.task:
Let's decorate the top of a receipt! Print the two lines below. Make the 12 = signs on the second line by repeating with *.
Ria Cafe
============
hints: Count the = signs on the second line again. There are 12 in all.
string * number repeated the string that many times. Remember the card that repeated “Ha” three times?
The first line is already there. Write one more print below it, and repeat = 12 times inside its parentheses.

print("Ria Cafe")
print("=" * ___)
items.explain: "=" * 12 made it without typing the same sign twelve times. Leave the counting to Python and you can't miscount.

items.q: Which statement about strings is true?
options: + joins two strings with no space between
* multiplies two strings and mixes them
Opening and closing quotes can differ
items.explain: + joins, and string * number repeats. Quotes must open and close with the same kind.

LESSONS.title: Doing math
summary: Numbers without quotes get calculated
/ gives decimals, // the quotient, % the remainder
** is a power; ( ) is calculated first

cards.say: Write numbers without quotes and Python does the math. Add with +, subtract with -, multiply with *, divide with /. Let's use it like a convenience store register!
There are three kinds of division. / gives the answer with decimals, // only the quotient, and % only the remainder. ** is a power, and anything in parentheses is calculated first.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Numbers without quotes really get calculated. The screen shows only the result, not the expression.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Wrapped in quotes, it's a string even if it looks like a number. So the two get joined instead of added.

items.q: Fill in the blank to get the total for paying the 1500 won bus fare 4 times.
items.explain: Python's multiply sign isn't x. It's the asterisk *.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Multiplication goes before addition. Do 3 * 4 = 12 first, then add 2 to get 14.

items.q: 5 friends share 17 candies equally. Fill in the blank to get how many are left over.
items.explain: Leftovers come from the remainder, %. // tells you each person's share, 3, and % tells you the 2 left over.

items.q: Put the lines in order so the output is 8, 2, 4.0.
items.explain: 2 ** 3 is three 2s multiplied together, 8, and 9 // 4 is the quotient 2. / adds a decimal point even when it divides evenly, like 4.0.

items.task:
At a convenience store you bought 2 triangle gimbap (seaweed-wrapped rice snacks) at 1200 won each and 1 milk at 1500 won. Don't type the total yourself: work it out with * and + and print it.
3900
hints: Look at what you bought again: 2 items at 1200 won and 1 item at 1500 won.
Multiply is *, add is +. Multiplication happens before addition.
Make one expression for the gimbap and one for the milk, then put a single expression that adds them inside print's parentheses.
items.explain: 1200 * 2 was calculated first, then 1500 was added. Thanks to the multiply-first rule, you didn't need parentheses.

items.q: Which expression gives 3?
items.explain: 7 // 2 is the quotient 3, 7 / 2 is 3.5, and 7 % 2 is the remainder 1. Tell the three division siblings apart and you're set.

LESSONS.title: Notes with comments
LESSONS.goal: Leave notes in your code with #
summary: Python doesn't read text after #
Comments are notes for people
Put # before a line to switch it off

cards.say: Text after a # sign is a comment. Python skips comments and doesn't read them. Think of it as a note to tomorrow's you.
Put # in front of a line you don't want to run, and that line takes a break. It's switched off without being deleted. But a # inside quotes is just a character.
cards.code:
# print("Pack an umbrella")
print("Pack sunscreen")
print("#WeatherToday")

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The first line starts with #, so it's a comment and gets skipped. The only line that runs is the print.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the first line becomes a note.
items.explain: Python's comment sign is a single #. In Python, // is the quotient (floor division) sign, and -- isn't a comment either, so both cause errors.

items.q: How many lines appear on screen when you run this code?
items.explain: The middle line has # at the very front, so the whole line is off. Only One and Three print: 2 lines.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: A # inside quotes is part of the string, so it prints as is. The comment runs from the # outside the quotes to the end of the line.

items.q: Read the end-of-line comments and put the lines in order: morning, lunch, evening.
items.explain: Text after # at the end of a line doesn't appear on screen, but it told the reader “when.” That's how comments work as notes.

items.task:
It's sunny today, so you don't need an umbrella. Don't delete the “Pack an umbrella” line; turn it into a comment so only this one line prints.
Pack sunscreen
hints: Right now two lines print. Which one don't you need today?
Putting # at the very start of a line made Python skip it. Remember the second card?
Just switch off the umbrella line. There was a way to make Python skip a line without deleting it.

___ print("Pack an umbrella")
print("Pack sunscreen")
items.explain: You switched the line off with # instead of deleting it. On a rainy day, remove just that one # and it's back on.

items.q: Which statement about comments is true?
options: Comments get printed on screen too
Comments can only go at the top of a file
items.explain: Comments are notes for people to read, so they're never run or printed. You can write them on any line.

LESSONS.title: Chapter 1 checkpoint
LESSONS.goal: Use print, strings, math and comments together
summary: print prints one line at a time, in order
Join strings with +, repeat them with *
Math goes without quotes; text after # is a note

cards.say: Time to wrap up Chapter 1! Here's everything you've learned, gathered on one screen. If you can tell what every line does, you're ready.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Inside quotes, even a math expression is just text. To calculate it, take away the quotes.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Do the multiplication 4 * 2 = 8 first, then subtract it from 20 to get 12. Going left to right gives 32, and that's the trap.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The second line is switched off with #. Overtime is commented out, and only Work prints.

items.q: Fill in the blank so “Lunch is gimbap” appears. (Gimbap is Korean rice rolls.)
items.explain: + joins the two strings as they are. With a comma, print adds one more space between them, so you'd get two spaces.

items.q: Turn 150 minutes into hours. Fill in the blank to get the minutes left over.
items.explain: 150 // 60 is 2 hours, and 150 % 60 is the 30 minutes left over. Remainders show up a lot in time math.

items.q: Which of these causes an error?
items.explain: A string + a number are different kinds, so they can't be added. Wrap 3 in quotes and they're both strings, so they join.

items.q: Put the lines in order for a receipt: shop name, divider, gimbap, latte, total.
items.expect:
Ria Cafe
--------
Gimbap 3000 won
Latte 4500 won
7500
items.explain: Output follows the order of the prints. * for the divider, + for joining and adding, # for notes: all of Chapter 1 on one screen.

items.task:
Let's make an intro card for new student Saessak (the name means “sprout”)! Print the three lines below exactly. Make the third line by repeating with *.
Name: Kim Saessak
Favorite drink: Iced tea
Go! Go! Go!

tests.expect:
Name: Kim Saessak
Favorite drink: Iced tea
Go! Go! Go!

hints: Look closely at the third line. There's a space after each “Go!”.
print prints one line at a time, and string * number repeats. Use those two things from Chapter 1 together.
Write one print per line. On the third line, find the one piece that repeats, and repeat just that piece.

# About me
print("Name: ___")
print("Favorite drink: ___")
print("___" * 3)
items.solution:
# About me
print("Name: Kim Saessak")
print("Favorite drink: Iced tea")
print("Go! " * 3)
items.explain: Three prints, and the repeating was left to *. Because you put the space inside the string, each Go! ends up exactly one space apart.

items.q: Which statement about Chapter 1 is true?
items.explain: "3" is a string, so * 2 repeats it into 33. 3 * 2 is 6, and 7 / 7 is 1.0, with a decimal point.

ADVANCED.title: Digits and alignment
ADVANCED.goal: Set decimal places and alignment with f-strings
summary: f"{value:format}": what follows : sets the look
.2f = 2 decimal places, , = thousands commas
< > ^ and a width align; a character before them fills

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. Remember f-strings from 1-2? Today we'll shape values with the characters after the colon inside { }.
cards.code:
print(f"A latte is {4500} won")
print(f"Pi is {3.14159:.2f}")
print(f"Total {4500 * 3:,} won")
cards.out:
A latte is 4500 won
Pi is 3.14
Total 13,500 won

cards.say: < aligns left, > right, ^ center, and the number is the width. One character before the align sign fills the empty space. Each character takes one space. Use a different kind of quote inside than outside.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: .2f shows only two digits after the decimal point. The third digit gets rounded, giving 3.14.

items.q: Fill in the blank so “2.50” appears.
items.explain: .2f keeps exactly two decimal places. 2f gives six decimal places (2.500000), and .2 keeps only two digits in total, giving 2.5.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Tea takes up 3 of the 6 characters of width, and > pushes it to the right. The 3 left over are filled with spaces on the left.

items.q: Fill in the blank so “1,500,000 won” appears.
items.explain: A comma after the colon puts a comma every three digits. .2f would add .00 after the decimal point, which is a different look.

items.q: Put the lines in order so the title, gimbap (Korean rice rolls) and latte come out lined up.
items.explain: Names sit left in a width of 8 and prices sit right in a width of 6, so the ends of the prices line up. The title is centered and filled with *.

items.task:
Line up two receipt lines with f-strings. Names: left-aligned, width 8. Amounts: right-aligned, width 8, with commas. Fill the empty space with . and calculate the second amount as 2500 * 5.
Cake.......4,500
Tea.......12,500
hints: Each line is a name column of 8 and an amount column of 8. Count how many dots went into each.
The character before the align sign filled the empty space, and amounts got the comma format. Combine the second card with the first.
Use two { } in one line. Put the name on the left (<) and the amount on the right (>), and write the second amount as an expression.
items.explain: Fill character, align sign, width and comma, all written together in one format spec. Even when the amount is an expression, the same format works just the same.

items.q: Which statement about format specs is true?
options: What follows the : inside { } sets the look
Values in { } go in even without the f
items.explain: Formats go inside an f-string's { }, after the colon. Without f, the { } prints as plain text, and ^ means center.

ADVANCED.title: Multi-line strings
ADVANCED.goal: Write several lines at once with triple quotes
summary: Open and close with three double quotes
Line breaks and blank lines print as written
Put f in front to add { } values too

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. Open and close with three double quotes, and you can write several lines as one string. Call print just once and the whole notice comes out.
cards.code:
print("""Today's menu
Latte 4500 won
Cake 5000 won""")
cards.out:
Today's menu
Latte 4500 won
Cake 5000 won

cards.say: Wherever you break a line in the code, the string breaks too, and blank lines stay. Break the line right after the opening quotes and you get a blank line on top. With f in front, { } works in multi-line strings too.

items.q: How many lines appear on screen when you run this code?
items.explain: Break the line inside triple quotes and that line break goes into the string. So you get two lines, A and B.

items.q: Fill in the blank to print a two-line menu.
items.explain: Multi-line strings open with three double quotes and close with three. Open with one or two and they don't match, so you get a SyntaxError clue.

items.q: How many lines appear on screen when you run this code?
items.explain: The blank line in the middle is part of the string, so it prints too. One, a blank line, Two: 3 lines.

items.q: What's the output of this code?
items.explain: If you open with three double quotes, you close with three. Close with just one and Python can't find where the string ends, so it gives you a clue.

items.q: How many lines appear on screen when you run this code?
items.explain: The line break right after the opening quotes goes into the string too. So there's a blank line on top: blank, Menu, Latte, 3 lines.

items.q: Put the lines in order so a three-line menu prints all at once.
items.explain: The line with the opening triple quotes goes first and the closing one goes last. The lines in between print in the order written.

items.task:
Print the notice with one multi-line f-string that opens with three double quotes. Calculate the total as 4500 * 3 and add the comma format. The second line is blank.
Today's set

Total 13,500 won
hints: The output has three lines, and the middle one is empty. The total has a comma in it.
Even in a multi-line string, putting f in front let you add values with { }. Remember the second card?
Open with three quotes, write line by line, and put the multiply expression and comma format only where the total goes.

print(f"""Today's set

Total {___ * 3:___} won""")
items.explain: Using f and triple quotes together put in the line breaks, the blank line and the calculated value all at once. The total is an expression, so it updates itself if the price changes.

items.q: Which statement about multi-line strings is true?
options: Open with three quotes, close with three
You can't put f in front
items.explain: Three quotes to open and three to close. Blank lines stay, and with f you can put in { } values too.

ADVANCED.title: Print a receipt
ADVANCED.goal: Print a receipt with format specs and multi-line strings
summary: Center the title with a fill character and ^
Names with <, amounts with > and a comma
Put dividers and math in a multi-line f-string

cards.say: One step further, last stop! We'll combine format specs and multi-line strings to print a receipt for gimbap (Korean rice rolls) and milk. Let's read the finished version first.
You can write expressions inside { }, so '-' * 13 makes the divider and 1500 * 2 works out the amount. For the title on top, center it with a fill character and ^.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the amount sits at the right of a width of 8, with a comma.
items.explain: Align sign, width, then comma, in that order. 8>, reads the 8 as the fill character, giving a different look, and >,8 is in the wrong order, so you get a clue.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Centering End in a width of 5 leaves one space on each side. The four = signs come from repeating with *.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Multiplication goes first: 1500 * 2 = 3000, plus 1200 makes 4200. The comma format splits off the thousands.

items.q: Put the lines in order for a receipt: title, gimbap, divider, total.
items.explain: In a multi-line f-string, the order you write the lines is the receipt's order: title, item, divider, total.

items.task:
Print the receipt with one multi-line string that opens with f""". Title: centered with = fill, width 15. Names: left, width 7. Amounts: right, width 8, with commas. The divider is '-' * 15, and the total is 4500 + 5000 * 2.
===Ria Cafe====
Latte     4,500
Waffle   10,000
---------------
Total    14,500
hints: There are five lines. Before picking a format for each one, reread the widths of the name and amount columns.
Fill-and-center, left-align, right-align with a comma, string * number, triple quotes: use everything from this Deep Dive.
The first line is started for you. Break lines inside the triple quotes, put { } on each line, and write the waffle amount and the total as expressions.
items.explain: Fill-and-center, alignment, commas, repetition and math, all in one multi-line f-string. When the leftover space is odd, like in the title, ^ gives the extra space to the right.

items.q: Which statement about printing receipts is true?
options: You can write expressions like '-' * 15 in { }
Align formats only work on strings
You can't use { } in multi-line strings
items.explain: You can write expressions like multiplication inside { }, and align formats work on numbers too. With f, { } works in multi-line strings as well.

TEMPLATES.explain: Multiplication goes before addition. {B} * {C} first, then add {A} → {OUT}

TEMPLATES.q: {K} people share {N} {FOOD} equally. Fill in the blank to get how many are left over.
TEMPLATES.explain: Leftovers come from the remainder, %. // gives each person's share, and / divides all the way into decimals.
Multiply a string by a number with * and it's joined that many times. So the screen shows {OUT}.

TEMPLATES.q: This code shows the price of {N} pieces of fruit. What's the output?
TEMPLATES.explain: With an f before the quotes, the expression inside { } is calculated and put between the words. Without f, or with the math outside { }, it prints as plain text.
